A polynomial is sketched below.


Which polynomial (in factored form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \(x-r\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at point \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[-6,\,-2,\,1,\,3,\,7\]

Thus, the factors are \(x+6\) and \(x+2\) and \(x-1\) and \(x-3\) and \(x-7\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x+6)^2(x+2)(x-1)^2(x-3)^2(x-7)\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(7\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading up. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is positive. This implies that \(a\) is positive. So, in this case, \(a=1\).

\[y=(x+6)^2(x+2)(x-1)^2(x-3)^2(x-7)\]

And then, since multiplication is commutative, the factors can be written in any order. In this case, the correct answer is:

\[y=(x+2)(x+6)^2(x-7)(x-3)^2(x-1)^2\]

Which polynomial (in factored form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \(x-r\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at point \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[-8,\,-6,\,-1,\,3\]

Thus, the factors are \(x+8\) and \(x+6\) and \(x+1\) and \(x-3\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x+8)^2(x+6)^2(x+1)^2(x-3)\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(3\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading down. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is negative. This implies that \(a\) is negative. So, in this case, \(a=-1\).

\[y=-(x+8)^2(x+6)^2(x+1)^2(x-3)\]

And then, since multiplication is commutative, the factors can be written in any order. In this case, the correct answer is:

\[y=-(x+8)^2(x+1)^2(x-3)(x+6)^2\]

Which polynomial (in factored form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \(x-r\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at point \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[-7,\,-4,\,2,\,8\]

Thus, the factors are \(x+7\) and \(x+4\) and \(x-2\) and \(x-8\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x+7)(x+4)^2(x-2)(x-8)^2\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(8\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading up. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is positive. This implies that \(a\) is positive. So, in this case, \(a=1\).

\[y=(x+7)(x+4)^2(x-2)(x-8)^2\]

And then, since multiplication is commutative, the factors can be written in any order. In this case, the correct answer is:

\[y=(x-2)(x+4)^2(x-8)^2(x+7)\]

Which polynomial (in factored form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \(x-r\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at point \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[2,\,4\]

Thus, the factors are \(x-2\) and \(x-4\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x-2)^2(x-4)\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(4\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading down. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is negative. This implies that \(a\) is negative. So, in this case, \(a=-1\).

\[y=-(x-2)^2(x-4)\]

And then, since multiplication is commutative, the factors can be written in any order. In this case, the correct answer is:

\[y=-(x-4)(x-2)^2\]

Let function \(f\) be a polynomial with real coefficients. If \(f(6+2i)=0\), then that implies that \(6+2i\) is one root of the polynomial.

What is the other known root?

When a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex root, we know the complex conjugate is also a root.

So, the answer is 6-2i

Let function \(f\) be a polynomial with real coefficients. If \(f(-8+6i)=0\), then that implies that \(-8+6i\) is one root of the polynomial.

What is the other known root?

When a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex root, we know the complex conjugate is also a root.

So, the answer is -8-6i

Let function \(f\) be a polynomial with real coefficients. If \(f(7-6i)=0\), then that implies that \(7-6i\) is one root of the polynomial.

What is the other known root?

When a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex root, we know the complex conjugate is also a root.

So, the answer is 7+6i

Let function \(f\) represent a standard-form quadratic polynomial shifted horizontally 4 units to the left.

\[f(x)=(x+4)^2-10(x+4)-11\]

Express function \(f\) in factored form.

Given: \[(x+4)^2-10(x+4)-11\]

Expand the squared binomial.

\[x^2+8x+16-10(x+4)-11\]

Distribute.

\[x^2+8x+16-10x-40-11\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2-2x-35\]

Factor.

\[(x+5)(x-7)\]

Let function \(f\) represent a standard-form quadratic polynomial shifted horizontally 2 units to the right.

\[f(x)=(x-2)^2+13(x-2)+40\]

Express function \(f\) in factored form.

Given: \[(x-2)^2+13(x-2)+40\]

Expand the squared binomial.

\[x^2-4x+4+13(x-2)+40\]

Distribute.

\[x^2-4x+4+13x-26+40\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2+9x+18\]

Factor.

\[(x+6)(x+3)\]

Let function \(f\) represent a standard-form quadratic polynomial shifted horizontally 7 units to the right.

\[f(x)=(x-7)^2+12(x-7)+27\]

Express function \(f\) in factored form.

Given: \[(x-7)^2+12(x-7)+27\]

Expand the squared binomial.

\[x^2-14x+49+12(x-7)+27\]

Distribute.

\[x^2-14x+49+12x-84+27\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2-2x-8\]

Factor.

\[(x+2)(x-4)\]

Let function \(f\) represent a standard-form quadratic polynomial shifted horizontally 2 units to the left.

\[f(x)=(x+2)^2-9(x+2)-10\]

Express function \(f\) in factored form.

Given: \[(x+2)^2-9(x+2)-10\]

Expand the squared binomial.

\[x^2+4x+4-9(x+2)-10\]

Distribute.

\[x^2+4x+4-9x-18-10\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2-5x-24\]

Factor.

\[(x+3)(x-8)\]

Let function \(f\) represent a standard-form quadratic polynomial shifted horizontally 7 units to the left.

\[f(x)=(x+7)^2-12(x+7)+11\]

Express function \(f\) in factored form.

Given: \[(x+7)^2-12(x+7)+11\]

Expand the squared binomial.

\[x^2+14x+49-12(x+7)+11\]

Distribute.

\[x^2+14x+49-12x-84+11\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2+2x-24\]

Factor.

\[(x+6)(x-4)\]
